lead: Multiply two powers of 2 and you land on another power of 2. That small fact carries this whole chapter: a set with an operation that never leaves the set, and that lets you regroup brackets without changing the answer. Add a do-nothing element and you have a monoid — the shape behind string building, matrix products and log buffers in code. Groups, the next step, demand one thing more: inverses.
prereq: You need: sets, subsets and function composition from Unit 2, Sets, Relations and Functions, plus the number systems ℕ, ℤ, ℚ and ℝ.

blocks.text: A binary operation ∗ on a set S is a rule that takes an ordered pair (a, b) of elements of S and returns exactly one element, written a ∗ b. Some books build closure into the definition by saying ∗ is a function from S × S to S; others state closure as a separate law. Both mean the same thing here: the answer must stay inside S.

Closure: for every a, b in S, the result a ∗ b also lies in S. On the positive integers ℤ⁺ = {1, 2, 3, …}, addition is closed, because a sum of two positive integers is positive. Subtraction is not closed: 3 − 5 = −2, and −2 is not in ℤ⁺. Division is not closed on ℤ either: 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6.
Associativity: (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c) for all a, b, c in S. Subtraction fails it: (5 − 3) − 1 = 1, while 5 − (3 − 1) = 3. Matrix multiplication is associative, and so is composition of functions.

blocks.where: a, b, c are any elements of the set S; ∗ is the binary operation on S.

blocks.text: Associativity lets you drop brackets: a ∗ b ∗ c is one well-defined element. Commutativity is a separate question. Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative: for A = [[1,1],[0,1]] and B = [[1,0],[1,1]], AB = [[2,1],[1,1]] while BA = [[1,1],[1,2]].
A semigroup is a pair (S, ∗) where ∗ is a binary operation on S that is closed and associative. Nothing more is demanded: no identity element, no inverses. Some syllabi spell it 'semi-group'.

items: (ℤ⁺, +): a sum of two positive integers is positive, and addition is associative. There is no identity, because 0 is not in ℤ⁺. This is a semigroup and not a monoid.
(Σ⁺, concatenation): Σ is an alphabet, say {a, b}, and Σ⁺ is the set of all non-empty strings over Σ. Joining two non-empty strings gives a non-empty string, and concatenation is associative.
(M₂(ℝ), ×): the 2 × 2 matrices with real entries. The product of two of them is again a 2 × 2 matrix with real entries, and matrix multiplication is associative.

blocks.text: The order of the pair matters: set first, operation second. Change the operation and the answer changes. (ℤ⁺, +) is a semigroup, but (ℤ⁺, −) is not even closed, and (ℤ, −) is closed yet not associative, so neither is a semigroup.
An identity element of (S, ∗) is an element e in S with e ∗ a = a ∗ e = a for every a in S. A monoid is a semigroup that has an identity. Some books write 'semigroup with identity' instead of monoid.

The identity is unique. Suppose e and f are both identities. Then e = e ∗ f, because f is an identity, and e ∗ f = f, because e is an identity. So e = f. A commutative monoid is a monoid whose operation is also commutative.

items: (ℕ₀, +) with ℕ₀ = {0, 1, 2, …}: identity 0, since 0 + a = a + 0 = a. Commutative monoid.
(Σ*, concatenation): all strings including the empty string ε. εw = wε = w, so ε is the identity. This monoid is called the free monoid on Σ.
(M₂(ℝ), ×): identity is I = [[1,0],[0,1]]. Matrix product is not commutative, so this is a monoid but not a commutative monoid.
(ℤ, ×): identity 1. The element 0 has no inverse, and a monoid is allowed to have such elements.

blocks.text: A submonoid is a subset T of a monoid (M, ∗) such that the identity e of M lies in T and T is closed under ∗. For example, the even numbers {0, 2, 4, …} form a submonoid of (ℕ₀, +): 0 is even, and a sum of two even numbers is even. Groups need one more axiom; see 4.2 Groups and subgroups.

figure.caption: The set of powers of 2 is closed under multiplication and has identity 1, but 2 has no inverse inside the set. The last block shows why the group test fails here.

spec.title: Monoid check for powers of 2
spec.aria: A downward flow checks closure, associativity and identity for M={1,2,4,8,...} and shows that 2 has no inverse in M.

examples.question: Let M = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …} = {2ⁿ | n ≥ 0} under ordinary multiplication. Show that M is a monoid but not a group. Use a = 3 and b = 5 to check closure.
steps: List the set: M = {2⁰, 2¹, 2², …} = {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …}. Every element is 2ⁿ with n a non-negative integer.
Closure: take 2ᵃ and 2ᵇ in M, so a ≥ 0 and b ≥ 0. Then 2ᵃ · 2ᵇ = 2ᵃ⁺ᵇ, and a + b ≥ 0, so the product is in M. Numerically with a = 3, b = 5: 2³ = 8 and 2⁵ = 32, and 8 × 32 = 256 = 2⁸, which is in M.
Associativity: multiplication of real numbers is associative, and M sits inside ℝ, so (2ᵃ · 2ᵇ) · 2ᶜ = 2ᵃ · (2ᵇ · 2ᶜ).
Identity: 1 = 2⁰ is in M, and 1 · 2ᵃ = 2ᵃ · 1 = 2ᵃ for every a ≥ 0. So 1 is the identity.
M is a semigroup with identity, hence a monoid. It is also commutative, since 2ᵃ · 2ᵇ = 2ᵃ⁺ᵇ = 2ᵇ⁺ᵃ = 2ᵇ · 2ᵃ, so it is a commutative monoid.
Inverse test: an inverse of 2 inside M would be an element x in M with 2 · x = 1, so x = 1/2 = 0.5. But every element 2ⁿ with n ≥ 0 satisfies 2ⁿ ≥ 1, so 0.5 is not in M.
The element 2 therefore has no inverse in M, so M fails the group axiom that every element is invertible.
examples.answer: M = {2ⁿ | n ≥ 0} is a commutative monoid with identity 1 = 2⁰, but 2 has inverse 0.5 ∉ M, so M is not a group.
examples.check:
a, b = 3, 5
print(2**a)
print(2**b)
print(2**a * 2**b)
print(2**(a + b))
print(2**0)
print(1 / 2)

traps: Checking only closure and associativity. A monoid also needs an identity. (ℤ⁺, +) is closed and associative but is only a semigroup, because 0 is missing.
Putting the identity outside the set. The even positive integers {2, 4, 6, …} under multiplication are closed and associative, but 1 is not in the set, so there is no monoid.
Forgetting the empty string. Σ* with concatenation is a monoid with identity ε; drop ε and Σ⁺ is only a semigroup.
Mixing up associative and commutative. Matrix multiplication is the standard counterexample: associative, not commutative.
Calling every monoid a group. A monoid may contain elements with no inverse, like 2 in the powers of 2, or 0 in (ℤ, ×).

quiz.a: A semigroup is a set with a binary operation that is closed and associative. A monoid is a semigroup that also has an identity element.

quiz.q: Give the identity element of (ℕ₀, +), (ℤ, ×) and (Σ*, concatenation).
quiz.a: 0 for (ℕ₀, +); 1 for (ℤ, ×); the empty string ε for (Σ*, concatenation).

quiz.q: Why is (ℤ⁺, +) a semigroup but not a monoid?
quiz.a: The sum of two positive integers is positive, and addition is associative, so it is a semigroup. The additive identity 0 is not a positive integer, so no identity lies in the set and it is not a monoid.

quiz.q: Let M = {3ⁿ | n ≥ 0} under multiplication. Show M is a monoid and name one element of M with no inverse in M.
quiz.a: Closure: 3ᵃ · 3ᵇ = 3ᵃ⁺ᵇ with a + b ≥ 0, so the product is in M. Associativity comes from multiplication of reals. Identity: 3⁰ = 1, and 1 · 3ᵃ = 3ᵃ. Hence a monoid. An inverse of 3 would be 1/3, and no 3ⁿ with n ≥ 0 equals 1/3, so 3 has no inverse in M.

quiz.q: S = {2, 4, 6, …} under multiplication is closed and associative. Is it a monoid? Which axiom fails, and show the failure.
quiz.a: It is not a monoid. The identity for multiplication is 1, and 1 ∉ S. No element of S can serve: the smallest candidate 2 gives 2 · 2 = 4 ≠ 2, so 2 is not an identity. S is a semigroup only.

quiz.q: Show that (ℤ, −) is not a semigroup.
quiz.a: Closure holds, since a difference of integers is an integer. Associativity fails: (5 − 3) − 1 = 1, but 5 − (3 − 1) = 3. Since 1 ≠ 3, subtraction is not associative, so (ℤ, −) is not a semigroup.

quiz.q: Let (M, ∗) be a monoid with identity e, and let T ⊆ M be closed under ∗ with e ∉ T. Is T a submonoid of M? Justify with an example.
quiz.a: No. A submonoid must contain the identity e of M. Example: the positive even integers {2, 4, 6, …} inside (ℕ₀, +). The sum of two of them is even, so T is closed, but 0 is missing, so the identity is absent and T is not a submonoid.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every append to a Python string or a log buffer is a monoid at work: append is associative and the empty string is the identity, which lets parallel workers merge partial results in any order. Functional programming uses the same word for exactly this reason, and folds over monoids parallelise for free. Formal language theory builds regular expressions over the free monoid Σ*. Search next for 'free monoid', 'monoid homomorphism' and 'monoid in Haskell'.
